title: Erie Canal Lock 23 to Lock 8
summary: Mid 70s, overcast, light winds, with canal sections at flood stage after five days of heavy rain.
body:
We departed Erie Canal Lock 23 at 0648 on September 23, 2021 aboard a Hatteras 75 Panacera, expecting this to be part of the home stretch into Troy and the final eastbound push on the Erie Canal.

But the canal had other ideas.

The previous five days had brought so much rain to the region that several sections were at flood stage. Around the locks, the dams were pushing huge amounts of water, and many of the downstream exits were far more turbulent than normal. Conditions for the day itself were not especially dramatic, mid-70s, overcast, light winds, but the canal system was clearly still carrying a lot more water than usual.

Even so, most of the day went smoothly.

The problem came just after Lock 8.

We approached a bridge we had passed under without issue on the westbound trip earlier that spring. As usual, the mate was in position on the ladder checking overhead clearance. Instead of the expected all-clear, he called down that we did not have room, and not by a little. We were somewhere around six to eight inches too tall for the bridge in the canal’s current state.

With current running and no interest in learning that lesson the expensive way, I brought the boat as close as I was comfortable to confirm it was real and not an optical illusion.

It was real.

We called the canal authority and reported the estimated clearance issue. They created an alert, and we turned around, locked back through Lock 8, and tied up on the calm side above the lock wall. After that, there was not much to do except let the system catch up.

So we secured the boat, talked with the lock master for a while, and then rode our electric scooters to the nearest restaurant for a decent lunch. Later we rode down the bike path to the bridge itself and took a few pictures of the water level. The lock master guessed they would have the canal dropped enough by around 0900 or 1000 the next morning.

At 0800 the next day we rode back to check it again and could already see how much difference the canal authority had made. It was actually impressive to watch that system do exactly what it was designed to do. We waited another hour just to be safe, then got underway again.

This time we had a little over two inches to spare.

We only made 74 nautical miles that day, and the canal bought itself one more day with us than we had planned on giving it. But it also reinforced a lesson that is easy to get lazy about in familiar water: procedure matters every time. It did not matter that we had already passed under that bridge months earlier. The mate checked clearance like he was supposed to, and that saved us from a very embarrassing and very expensive mistake.

title: Flying Fish Marina to Staniel Cay
summary: A long calm run from Long Island back toward Staniel Cay got Lady B back on schedule, with whales on departure and an improvised trolling session at the cut while waiting for the slip to open.
body:
We departed Flying Fish Marina in Clarence Town, Long Island, on March 20, 2023 aboard *Lady B*, an 85-foot Pacific Mariner, bound for Staniel Cay.

This was the last long passage with the owner and guests still aboard at the tail end of a months-long Bahamas trip. Weather had already delayed our departure by a couple of days, which killed the original plan of working our way back north by shorter island-hopping legs. The guests had departure flights out of Nassau coming up, so we needed to cover a big section of the southern Exumas in one shot and get them back into the neighborhood for the final few days of the trip.

It turned into exactly the kind of day you hope for when the schedule has started to tighten.

Conditions on departure were 76.8°F with light SSE winds around 9 knots. By arrival they had shifted slightly to about 10 knots from the SSW, temperature 74.7°F, with calm seas all day. The gentle wind stayed at our back, the boat ran well, and the guests were actually able to enjoy the day instead of spending it stressed about timing or beat up by weather.

We saw whales on departure, then settled into a smooth run up the sound. By the end of the day we had covered 113 nautical miles in just under nine hours.

The only wrinkle came at Staniel. When we got to the cut, I called Patrice on the radio and found out our slip at the marina was not cleared out yet. She asked if we could give it another hour before coming in.

So we turned around and improvised.

The guests rigged some lines and we went trolling with an 85-foot motoryacht, which is not the most dignified look but got the job done. We ended up landing a four-foot barracuda, which was also the day I learned that our deckhand’s fishing skills were mostly fictional. Fortunately the chef was a real fisherman and stepped in, handled the whole thing cleanly, got the trophy photos, and saw to it that the fish was safely released.

That killed just enough time for our slip to open up. We got into the marina, got everything unstowed, and had the boat settled in time for dinner.

What I remember most about that day is how pleasant it was in spite of the schedule pressure hanging behind it. No weather, no drama, no guest anxiety, just a smooth run, a little improvisation at the end, and the feeling that we had gotten back on schedule without anybody having to suffer for it. After a long trip, that kind of day stands out.

title: New York Harbor Arrival on Lady Victory
summary: Took command less than a day before departure from Florida, learned the boat underway, then entered New York Harbor on the first nice June weekend with the radar finally back online and a screen full of traffic.
body: I took command of the boat less than 24 hours before departure from Florida and had to learn it all the way up the coast. A few low sleep days into my command we were passing under the Verrazzano Bridge into lower New York Harbor. I had finally repaired the radar and plotter, and it was the first nice June weekend day in New York, so when I entered the harbor the spiderweb of target tracks that appeared on the screen made for a distinct change in operation from the offshore Atlantic run of the previous few days.

title: Crossing to Chub Cay
summary: Seed example log entry for a South Florida to Bahamas crossing day, structured to power both homepage recents and Travel Trail archive views.
body:
This is a seed example log entry, meant to prove the content model rather than claim a final polished narrative.

Left South Florida on a clean enough weather window and settled into the crossing rhythm, the kind where the job becomes less about talking and more about paying attention. The point of a log like this in the system is not just to hold prose, but to pin a dated movement to real places, a real chapter arc, and supporting images that can back up the memory later.

As the run moved east, the crossing stopped being an abstract line on a map and became the emotional hinge between familiar water and island water. That is exactly the kind of transition the archive should be able to show, not only in photos, but in written material that can appear on the homepage as a recent log and still live permanently inside the full Travel Trail archive.

Arrival at Chub Cay gives the entry a clear destination anchor, but the important structural point is that this one log can relate to Fort Lauderdale, the crossing itself, Chub Cay, the Exploration Years chapter, and multiple images without duplicating anything.

title: Boca to Boca, With a Steering Problem in the Middle
summary: Around 80°F with light SSE wind, good conditions for an easy owner day cruise.
body:
We departed The Boca Raton on March 24, 2025 aboard *Lady Victory* for what was supposed to be a simple owner cruise, a pleasant run out of the home slip, down toward Fort Lauderdale, and back. The plan was easy enough: ICW to Hillsboro Inlet, out to the ocean, back in through Port Everglades, then a relaxed ride north on the ICW to Boca. Conditions were good, around 80 degrees with light SSE wind, and nothing about the day suggested it was going to become particularly educational.

For the most part, it did not.

The owners had friends aboard and were just out for a boat ride. While we were offshore between Pompano and Fort Lauderdale, I handed the wheel to the mate so I could do a quick engine room check and step away for a minute. When I came back up, he showed me that the rudder indicator was no longer responding to wheel input. The boat was still tracking straight and we were only making about five to six knots, but it was immediately clear that something in the steering system was no longer behaving normally.

I went back down to the engine room and found the reservoir for the power steering pump empty.

I topped it off, repressurized the system, and confirmed over the radio with the mate that steering response had returned. That got us moving normally again, and we continued into Port Everglades. While we were waiting on the Las Olas bridge, I went back down and found the reservoir about halfway drained again. So from there on out, the trip became a quiet exercise in keeping the system alive long enough to get home cleanly. I kept adding fluid, kept checking levels, and kept us moving.

From the guest side, it was still just a nice day on the boat.

That was the whole point.

We completed the trip and made it back to the slip without the owners or their guests ever really knowing there had been an issue. The main challenge, other than the actual steering problem, was trying to keep my uniform looking vaguely presentable while repeatedly disappearing to deal with power steering fluid.

Once we were back, I told the boss what had happened and went straight into the lazarette to find the missing fluid. It was not hard to locate. Most of it was in the bilge, and the source turned out to be a steering hose that had very nearly ruptured completely. That afternoon I had new steering lines made, and the mate and I replaced them.

What stays with me about that day is that from the outside it looked like nothing had happened. Sometimes that is what a successful day actually looks like. Not heroics, not drama, just finding the problem, managing it calmly, and getting everybody home before the issue gets a chance to introduce itself properly.

title: New York to Portsmouth Instead of Virginia Beach
summary: Departure cold but calm; arrival cold and blowing, with seas building near the mouth of the Chesapeake.
body:
We departed Chelsea Piers in New York on the evening of October 7, 2025 aboard *Lady Victory*, starting south on the seasonal delivery run out of the city. The original destination was the Virginia Beach Fishing Center.

By the time we left, we were already a few days behind schedule. The boat had mechanically protested getting underway in the first place, and the weather window was starting to narrow. Departure from New York Harbor was cold but calm, and for most of the overnight run the trip was fairly uneventful.

As morning came on, the weather started to shift.

We were in contact with Virginia Beach Fishing Center as we approached. That inlet can be unpredictable even on a good day, and they were already reporting shoaling. Local traffic moving through was still giving usable guidance on where the safe water was, and based on those reports we were not especially worried about our 5.5-foot draft. At that stage, getting in still looked possible.

But the closer we got, the less attractive that plan became.

Near the mouth of the Chesapeake, with Virginia Beach only another hour to hour and a half away, the seas were continuing to build and the forecast for the next few days was looking worse, not better. Even if we got in, there was a good chance we would be stuck there for several days. And once the weather passed, there was no telling what the shoaling at the inlet would look like afterward. We were close enough to make it work, but no longer close enough to justify it.

So we changed the plan and diverted to Tidewater Yacht Marina in Portsmouth instead.

It was the safer option, the more stable option, and it also set us up well for the next day. With weather shutting down the outside route anyway, Portsmouth positioned us to continue south on the ICW instead of gambling on a sketchy arrival and then sitting around trapped behind worsening conditions.

We did not get tied up until around midnight, so it made for a long day. But it was still the right call. Better to end tired in the right place than spend the night congratulating yourself for forcing the original plan.

That run stands out because there was no dramatic emergency, just the steady narrowing of a bad option until the smarter one became obvious. Those are the decisions that keep trips moving.

title: Barry at Shroud Cay
summary: Night watch on the ball at Shroud Cay became one of the most peaceful parts of the trip, with a resident barracuda in the lights and a silence that made the world feel older again.
body:
One of the most peaceful memories I carried away from that trip came from doing something that was technically work.

We were on the ball at Shroud Cay, and the owners wanted to hear me walking the deck every hour through the night. So I kept making my rounds, again and again, while the boat sat alone in the mooring field.

That should have made it feel like a duty.

Instead, it became one of the best parts of the trip.

Every time I came out, my buddy Barry, a barracuda who hunted the edges of the underwater lights, was there in the glow like he had the watch too. I started expecting him. The night had that kind of rhythm to it, where even something a little sharp-toothed starts to feel like part of the company.

But what really made it stay with me was the quiet.

No ambient light. No background noise. No endless shore glow from roads, houses, marinas, or condos. Just the boat, the water, the stars, and whatever else was moving around out there in the dark. The sky was so clear it almost felt unreasonable, like there was more of it than you were supposed to be able to see at once.

And in that kind of quiet, it is hard not to feel connected to the people who moved through places like that hundreds of years ago, before everything got paved over and built up and lit to death. Out there, for a little while, the world feels older again.

Nighttime at Shroud Cay, when you are the only boat in the mooring field, is one of the most peaceful places I have ever been.

title: The Water Color Change Crossing into the Bahamas
summary: The water color change on the crossing is the signal that operations, pace, and guest service are about to change, and it is even better when the dolphins show up.
body: The color change of the water as you cross the Gulf Stream and finally arrive in the Bahamas is a signal that operations are changing and we're transitioning to visual navigation, a slower pace, and full press guest service. It's even better when the dolphins show up to greet us.

title: Welcome Home at Compass Cay
summary: The weathered hand-painted sign on the final turn into Compass Cay harbor still hits like a genuine welcome from people who mean it.
body:
Every time I pull into Compass Cay, the **Welcome Home** sign gets me.

It is weathered, hand-painted, and sitting on the starboard side as you enter the harbor. After you work your way around the entrance channel and round that last corner, there it is waiting for you as you come in.

Maybe that is part of why it lands so well. You do not just happen to notice it. You earn the sight of it a little.

And every time I see it, it makes my heart feel happy.

Part of that is the place itself, but a bigger part is the people. The guys there have a way of making you feel like you are part of their home, and they do it genuinely, not as a performance and not as some polished act meant to keep people coming back. It feels real. That is the difference.

There are plenty of beautiful stops in the Bahamas, and plenty of places that know how to be charming. Compass Cay stays with me because it feels welcoming in a deeper way than that. It does not feel like you are arriving at a destination. It feels like you are being received.

That is why it has become one of my favorite stops overall.

title: The Time I Tested the Hair Dye
summary: A volunteer hair-dye test to calm the boss before her boyfriend arrived solved the problem and left Tommy looking accidentally presidential for far longer than expected.
body:
Near the end of a three-month trip, the boss’s boyfriend was due to join the boat for the last couple of weeks. That meant preparations, and among them was one very specific problem: her hairstylist had sent her along with the proper coloring so she could find a local salon and get touched up before he arrived.

Only there was no local hairdresser available where we were, and he was arriving the next day.

So the plan changed. The stew was going to do it.

That was fine right up until it became real. Just before they started, the boss began questioning whether this was actually a good idea. I happened to be walking through the galley while that discussion was going on, and I could feel the uncertainty building. So I offered the only solution that seemed useful at the time.

The stew could use me as the practice canvas first.

If she did a terrible job, I could always shave my head. The boss, understandably, did not have that option.

She looked slightly stunned that I would volunteer for this, but she accepted. So there I was, seated for an unofficial hair-color trial, reading the instructions from the professional while the stew more or less ignored them and did it her own way. I was not the best patient, mostly because I could see in real time that “her way” and “the actual directions” were not especially aligned.

Still, in the end, she did a good job. The boss was reassured, the real coloring went ahead, and she looked good for the boyfriend’s arrival.

My hair, on the other hand, came out looking like **The Donald**.

At first it was just funny and a little absurd. But the best part came later, after we got back to the States. By then I had mostly adapted to it, or maybe just stopped noticing. Then I went to my usual barber, and she started laughing the second she saw me. Fortunately for me, part of her training was fixing bad dye jobs, so she managed to make me look more normal again. Even then, it took a long time before the last of it finally grew out.

For a while I looked like a man with an unhealthy devotion to the boss’s exact hair color. It solved the problem, though, which is why I still think it was worth it.

title: The Night Door County Claimed Me Back
summary: A private sendoff at a Door County restaurant turned a seasonal stop into proof that the place and its people had become part of Tommy's life for real.
body:
My time in Door County stayed with me for a lot of reasons, but one night near the end of the season holds the whole place together in my mind.

I was getting ready to head back down to Florida for the winter, and one of the locals decided to hold a private event at his restaurant for me before I left. The first thing I remember is the sign out front: **Closed for a Private Event**.

That alone would have been enough to make me stop.

But then I walked in and realized everyone there was there for a reason, and that was not a normal night in that place.

No tourist noise. No seasonal circus. Just the locals.

That was what made it feel so meaningful. Door County has that real Midwestern character, the kind that is not flashy and does not need to explain itself. Over time those people had gone from familiar faces to real friends, and that night made it impossible to pretend the connection was one-sided.

It felt good to be celebrated like that. Good in a way that is a little hard to admit cleanly, because most of the time you just keep moving and do the work and assume you passed through a place the way you pass through most places. But that night made me realize they appreciated me as much as I appreciated them.

That is not something you forget.

There are true friends still in that part of the world, and I still long to see them again. That sendoff gave Door County a permanent place in me.

title: Gulf Stream Window Rule
summary: Seed example note entry showing how quick operational truths or remembered fragments can support logs, stories, places, and image-backed archive navigation.
body:
This is a seed example note entry.

A note like this exists for the kind of truth that is too useful to lose and too small to force into a full story. The crossing never cares what the calendar says. What matters is whether the day feels right, whether the window is real, and whether the sea state matches the optimistic story people tell themselves at the dock.

In the archive model, a note like this should be able to sit under the crossing place, connect to a log entry, and attach to one or more supporting images. That makes it useful both as a piece of seamanship memory and as part of the broader narrative graph.

title: A Boat Can Be Beautiful and Still Be Sick
summary: Cosmetic presentation can hide tired systems, normalized dysfunction, and warning signs that only look normal to people who do not yet know better.
body:
Exterior presentation tells you something about a program, but it does not tell you everything. A neglected exterior often does foreshadow what you are about to find inside, but even that is not always reliable. Sometimes a rough-looking boat surprises you. And sometimes a perfectly manicured yacht tied up at the dock, polished and shining and giving every outward sign of competence, is already trying to tell you something is wrong the moment you step aboard.

Usually it starts with smell.

If the interior smells like mold, blackwater, stale humidity, or some other version of trapped system failure, that is the first sign. Then you start hearing things. A pump laboring. A fan motor struggling. An air handler that sounds tired. Lights dimming when they should not. A toilet flush that drags voltage down like the boat is negotiating with itself.

To owners and guests, that world is often completely foreign. They may assume all boats smell that way. They may assume everybody gets bronchitis after spending a week aboard. They may assume pumps, air conditioners, and heads all sound like they are barely hanging on because they have no better reference point. Even crew can fall into the same trap if all they have known is less-than-stellar boats. Once dysfunction becomes familiar, people start calling it normal.

It is not normal.

That is one of the harder parts of experience. You stop hearing just noise and start hearing symptoms. You stop seeing a beautiful boat and start noticing the signs that the systems underneath it are tired, neglected, or already in decline. That is also when the captain’s life gets more difficult, because eventually you have to tell an owner that something major needs to be addressed, and the answer you often get back is, “It’s always worked that way.”

Until it doesn’t.

A lot of expensive surprises aboard yachts are only surprising to the people who got used to the warnings.

title: Check the Whole Interior Before Casting Off
summary: Never depart the dock, no matter how short the run, without checking the full interior, even if you know you were the last person through those spaces.
body:
Never depart the dock, no matter how short the trip is, without checking the entire interior, even if you know you were the last person in those spaces.

An owner bought a new tender and it was at the dealership's service slip, and I was sent to move it to the owner's house. It was just a short smooth water run in a new boat. I went through all my mechanical checks, did a quick deck sweep, and staged lines and fenders for a quick landing on arrival.

Apparently the owner's kids had put together a congratulations gift in the V berth, a serving tray on the foot of the bed with several bottles of red wine and crystal stemware. None of it made sense as something the kids would ever actually use or probably ever even see in the tender V berth, but they did it anyway. The surprise was found by the crew smashed on the floor with red wine painting the lower sections of the walls and shards of high end wine glass everywhere.

So I never cast off without checking the whole interior.

title: Checklists Exist to Replace Assumption with Knowledge
summary: The value of a checklist is not paperwork but verified reality, and lifejackets make the point better than most systems do.
body:
Checklists matter because they replace assumption with accountability.

Having procedures means we get to operate knowing something is ready, not just hoping it probably is. That distinction sounds small right up until it isn’t.

That is true across the boat, but safety gear makes the point especially well. Lifejacket checks become repetitive, and because they are repetitive, people start treating them as automatic. The assumption becomes that the number of lifejackets in the locker has not changed because nobody has used one, moved one, borrowed one, or left one in some other compartment. But that is still just an assumption.

Actually opening the locker, visually checking them, and counting them does something important. It turns “they should be there” into “we know they are there.” It also confirms they are not tangled up, buried, damaged, or otherwise not ready to use when the time comes.

That is the real value of a checklist.

It is not there to create paperwork. It is there to force someone to verify reality before reality gets a vote. In a real emergency, you do not want to be untangling lifejackets, discovering one is missing, or deciding in real time who does not get one. By then the checklist has already failed, and so have the people responsible for it.

Good procedures are not about looking organized. They are about removing guesswork from the moments when guesswork becomes expensive.

title: Do Not Trust the Blackwater System Just Because Someone Logged It
summary: Blackwater systems are often the first neglected system on a new boat, which is exactly why they need immediate eyes-on verification regardless of what the service logs claim.
body:
MSD and blackwater systems are some of the first things I worry about when joining a new boat, because they are also some of the first things previous crews tend to avoid until avoidance is no longer an option.

That pattern has repeated itself often enough that I no longer treat service logs as proof that the system is healthy. On both *Lady B* and *Lady Victory*, the blackwater system ended up giving me a very direct education in what these systems actually need in order to function properly, how quickly small neglect turns into a disgusting operational problem, and how often people convince themselves that if the toilets still sort of work, the system must be fine.

It usually is not.

Nobody likes dealing with human waste. That is exactly why these systems get neglected. They are unpleasant, out of sight when they are behaving, and easy to postpone in favor of more visible jobs. But ignoring the system that handles waste is not a strategy. It is just a delayed emergency.

At this point, when I join a boat, blackwater is one of the systems I want eyes on early, no matter what the paperwork says. The first things I want checked are the transfer pump, the hoses, and the chemical pump and reservoir. I also want a proper dose of the correct tank treatment to make sure the biology is balanced from the start. Those are first-step items every time.

I want to know what has actually been serviced, what has only been claimed, what is close to failure, and what bad habits have been normalized around it. If you wait until the boat is full, the guests are aboard, or the tank is at capacity, you are already late.

The lesson is simple: if the waste system looks like something nobody wants to think about, that is probably because nobody has been thinking about it.

title: Weather Does Not Care Who Your Dinner Guests Are
summary: Part of the captain's job is standing up to owner pressure when the weather answer is no, because schedule pressure does not change conditions.
body:
Sometimes part of the job is standing up to the boss.

There is a reason they need you, and one of those reasons is that somebody on board has to care more about reality than about the owner’s preferred outcome. Weather is one of the clearest examples.

Weather windows are not a formality. They are not a suggestion, and they are not something you get to negotiate with because the schedule became inconvenient. If a major system is moving through, if the conditions are unsafe, or if the risk has crossed the line from manageable to foolish, then that is the answer. Not the beginning of a debate.

Owners can try every tactic in the book when they do not like that answer. Schedule pressure, guest pressure, sunk-cost pressure, irritation, status, guilt, confidence, the belief that money should be able to bend circumstances, all of it shows up sooner or later. None of it changes the weather.

Mother Nature does not care that dinner guests are only in town for one more night. She does not care what was promised, what was planned, or how badly somebody wants the evening to go a certain way. She is not involved in the negotiation.

And neither should you be, once the answer is clear.

If you are the person responsible for the boat and the people aboard, then sometimes your job is to disappoint somebody on purpose. Better that than pretending conditions are acceptable just because the boss is not in the mood to hear otherwise.

We are not going out in a named storm.

title: A Better Night in Staniel Cay
summary: What started as one more charter-season night beside a burned-out neighboring crew turned into a real Staniel Cay memory when a local Junkanoo wedding procession transformed the Yacht Club and revealed the island's living culture.
body:
I was in Staniel Cay sometime around mid-March or early April, at that point in the season when the spring-break charter grind was starting to wind down and everyone looked a little used up.

A boat across the dock from us had apparently just finished its final charter. The guests had flown out, their captain had quit that same day, and what remained was a crew at the end of its rope with no supervision and a relief captain not arriving until the next morning. They descended on the Yacht Club bar exactly the way you would expect.

There had already been some interaction with my boss at dinner that left her completely over the whole group. We finished eating, went back to the boat, and my bosses decided they had had enough for one night. They told me to go enjoy myself if I wanted, since they were turning in early and planned to sleep late the next morning.

So I walked back over to the Yacht Club.

By then, fortunately, the crew from hell had mostly drank themselves into retreat and wandered back to their quarters. The place had settled down again. Carl made me a drink, and I sat for a minute in what had become a genuinely mellow, peaceful little scene, figuring I would enjoy one quiet moment and then head to bed myself.

Then the whole night changed.

A wedding procession came through with a local Junkanoo group leading the way. They looped through the Yacht Club bar with the wedding party and carried the celebration back outside toward the restaurant for the reception. The shift was instant. What had been a quiet bar became a room full of people celebrating the couple, moving to the music, and getting pulled into the energy of it.

The band was incredible, full of instruments that looked and sounded nothing like the usual polished tourist version of island music. The locals were in costume and performing, but it never felt commercial or dutiful. It did not feel like people putting on a show because guests expected one. It felt like they were carrying something forward because it mattered to them, because it belonged to the place, and because they were proud to represent their culture as ambassadors rather than hired actors.

That was what stayed with me.

After the performance, a lot of them came back in for refreshments, drenched in sweat and looking like they had given everything they had to it. I ended up spending time with them, and the more I talked with them, the more obvious it became how proud they were to carry on those traditions and share them with people visiting the island. It told me more about Staniel Cay in one evening than a week of postcards ever could.

What I expected to be a brief nightcap turned into one of those nights where a place stops being just another stop and becomes something more personal. I met people I became genuinely close with, and I came away understanding something real about the island and the people who call it home.

I slept great that night. By the time my bosses woke up the next morning, the floating asylum across the dock had disappeared, the whole mood had reset, and somehow the sun really did seem to shine a little brighter.

It started as one of those charter-season nights that makes you think humanity may have peaked a while ago, and ended as one of the more genuinely Bahamian experiences I have had.

title: The Glamorous Life, Staniel Cay Edition
summary: A boss's birthday trip, sixteen people aboard, a dead-headed Y valve, a destroyed waste pump, a bidet geyser in the master, and an emergency pump flown into Staniel to save a three month charter from ending in week two.
body:
On Lady B in the Bahamas, it was the boss's birthday trip with fourteen women aboard, plus the deckhand and me as the only two males. On arrival to Staniel we discovered that the plumber at Rolly, who had serviced the MSD, hooked up a Y valve wrong. So not only was the black water tank at capacity and close to overflow, the main waste transfer pump tried to cycle against a hose that dead ended into the closed side of the improperly installed valve. The result was a pump that destroyed itself and a full waste tank with sixteen guests aboard.

After an all hands announcement telling everyone the heads were not to be flushed and to use the marina facilities, apparently a couple of the women thought this didn't apply to them and they used the toilets anyway, causing a geyser in the master stateroom through the bidet, which also had a check valve improperly installed.

I found a pump in Fort Lauderdale, had a friend bring it to FXE and put it on the next Makers Air flight to Staniel Cay, jumped through all the Bahamian government hoops to get an import license, received the replacement pump that afternoon, and installed it in the in-flight jet engine repair method, which required me to participate in an enclosed space with an active crap volcano flowing. I also had to rework the Y valve with full waste pipes.

I didn't smell pretty, but the system was repaired and functional and we didn't have to end the trip two weeks into the three month plan. The repair held, and I eventually smelled better. The epitome of the glamorous life of crewing on a yacht in paradise.

title: Fourth of July in Sag Harbor, Because Apparently That Was the Plan
summary: A last-minute owner request turned a Chelsea Piers standby into a holiday sprint to Sag Harbor, a dressed-out mooring-ball hosting operation, and a full run back to Manhattan by the next evening.
body:
In July 2025 I was on *Lady Victory*, tied up at Chelsea Piers in Manhattan. The owners had been traveling most of June, and we were not supposed to be in the Hamptons yet. That was an August plan. No dockage had been arranged, no Fourth of July setup existed, and under normal circumstances none of this would have been attempted on a holiday weekend.

Then on July 3rd I got the call asking if we could move the boat to Sag Harbor so they could watch the fireworks.

Under ideal conditions it is about a seven-hour run. This was not ideal. The Fourth landed on a Friday, which meant peak summer weekend, prime destination, and the sort of availability problem that usually gets solved long before the day before. I started calling around anyway. Most of my contacts in Sag Harbor laughed, which was a reasonable reaction, but eventually somebody found me a mooring ball.

That was enough to turn the day from impossible into merely stupid.

The crew's first reaction was basically, no chance this can play. By the end of the day it had turned into, I think we might actually pull this off.

And to their credit, they did.

By the time we got to Sag Harbor, *Lady Victory* was standing tall on the mooring because the crew had pulled out all the stops. We had no chef, so everything had to be picked up in town during setup. Our stew grabbed Fourth of July decorations in Manhattan before we left, and by that night there were flags strung up everywhere and the interior actually looked better than the whole operation had any right to. The boss did not seem to notice, but it looked good.

Guest transfers were exactly the kind of mess you would expect from a last-minute holiday plan involving wealthy people and a waterfront town. Everyone seemed to arrive at once and expected to be shuttled out immediately. Several went to the wrong dock despite having perfectly good directions, which they apparently found too burdensome to follow. At one point the stew ran back into town on the shuttle boat for provisions, then got trapped trying to return because the public shuttle dock had turned into a complete mob scene.

There were plenty of small hiccups through setup, but by fireworks time we had done it. We hosted the evening, got everyone where they were supposed to be, and gave the owners their Sag Harbor Fourth of July as if this had all been sensibly arranged in advance.

For us, it was a grind. We were exhausted. But there was one unexpected reward: that night on the mooring was the first time since leaving Florida that we were not being constantly rocked by ferry wake. It was a short night, but all of us woke up saying it was the first good sleep we had had in weeks.

The next morning we came off the mooring, fueled at Sag Harbor Yacht Club, and ran all the way back to Chelsea Piers. By 6 p.m. we were back in Manhattan, like none of this had been an unreasonable request in the first place.

It was a ridiculous twenty-four hours, most of it was inconvenient for everyone involved except the guests, and by the end of it we were exhausted. But we pulled it off, got a decent night of sleep for the first time since leaving Florida, and made it back to New York feeling like we had gotten away with something.

title: The Day Lake Michigan Pretended to Be a Millpond
summary: After decades of making the Bay Harbor to Holland run, Tommy got the rarest version of Lake Michigan, over a hundred miles of early-spring water so flat it made the Manitou Passage lighthouse reflection look unreal.
body:
I got called to run a boat from Bay Harbor down to Holland, Michigan. It was a small boat, but we still had a crew of three because Lake Michigan can turn on you quickly, and extra hands are never a bad thing on a real run. It was early spring, which only adds to the uncertainty. The lake is still waking up then, and you do not assume kindness just because the dock looks calm.

I have been making versions of that trip since I was fourteen years old.

That day, Lake Michigan did something I had never seen before.

We ran more than a hundred miles without seeing a real ripple on the water. Not a calm patch here and there, not just a lucky morning, but a full day of the lake lying down so completely it almost looked fake. The boat was running so flat you could barely feel the speed. There was none of the usual effort in it. We were just moving, level and clean, across water that looked more like polished glass than one of the Great Lakes.

There are pictures from that run of the Manitou Passage lighthouse where the reflection is so perfect it looks like it is hanging in space. That was the whole feeling of the day. Suspended. Slightly unreal.

What made it hit even harder was the time of year. It was cold. I do not remember seeing other pleasure boats out there, maybe only a couple of freighters farther offshore than our route. The trees along shore were just starting to bud, with that thin early green you only notice because so much else is still gray. Most of the shoreline was bare trunks and muted woods, broken up by the sand dunes standing out more clearly without summer leaves on the trees. It felt empty, but not dead. More like the lake and the shoreline were in the first stage of waking back up.

That feeling matters up there.

Every spring on Lake Michigan carries a sense that you made it through another one. The desolation, the ice, the snow, the long gray stretch of winter, all of it takes a toll. Early spring is not alive yet, not fully, but your first real leg up or down the lake brings back that sense of anticipation. You know the season is starting to turn. In a couple months everything will flip and the harbors will be full, the transients will pile in, and if you live there long enough you may already be looking ahead to when it quiets back down again. The shoulder seasons are short, and that is part of why they mean so much.

That day felt like Lake Michigan briefly performing as imagined by people who have never actually been on it. Outsiders like to picture the Great Lakes as oversized ponds, calm and easy. Anyone who knows them knows better. Which is why getting a day where the lake really did look like a millpond, after dozens of runs on the same route, felt so rare.

It was a once-in-a-lifetime run.

I would gladly do that trip again tomorrow, but I would not expect to get that lake twice.

title: The Thirteen-Foot Whaler Years
summary: Seed example story entry for the Home Waters arc, showing how longer memory-driven narrative can sit beside logs and notes in the same connected archive.
body:
This is a seed example story entry, meant to show how the archive can hold memory and narrative, not just dated movement.

The thirteen-foot Whaler years belong to the beginning, not because they were small, but because they were foundational. A boat like that is remembered differently when it is not a toy or a novelty, but a real way of learning water, distance, weather, and confidence. That is the kind of material that should live under a chapter like Home Waters Runs, even if it does not behave like a single-day log.

A story entry like this gives the system room for memory, reflection, and continuity. It can connect to South Florida places, to a broader life arc, and to representative images, while still remaining distinct from a dated passage log or a short operational note.

This is also where the archive starts to become more than a photo browser. The image may help trigger the memory, but the story gives the picture meaning, context, and emotional weight.

title: The Sound System Worked Great
summary: A first move on a newly purchased yacht revealed everything backwards at once: stereo upgrades before assessment, dead controls, harbor-arrest insurance restrictions, and a chapter defined by good bones buried under neglect and bad priorities.
body:
A new owner flew me and a few support crew down to take over her newly purchased first yacht. Before we even reached the boat, the tone was already starting to set. We boarded her private jet, and the engineer had turned the cabin of a Lear 75 into a traveling tool crib, with toolboxes stacked down the center aisle.

We landed in West Palm Beach, took an Uber to Palm Harbor Marina, and expected to board the boat and head more or less straight for Fort Lauderdale. The seller had already cancelled the slip, so the plan on paper was simple: get aboard, do the basics, and move the boat south to the yard for assessment and refit.

When I first stepped aboard, the boat did not feel like a lost cause. It felt like it had once been a good boat. But sometime after the original crew was fired and the boat was put on the market, it had spent more than a year sitting without real crew aboard while a management company allegedly looked after it, billed for it, and mostly ignored it. It had that particular feeling some boats get when the bones are still there but the stewardship has gone missing.

Then we found a stereo crew already aboard.

Apparently the owner had decided the most urgent improvement this newly purchased yacht needed before heading to the yard for assessment was an upgraded exterior sound system. Contracts had already been signed. Nobody had mentioned that little detail to me in advance.

That was the first real red flag.

We waited for the stereo installers to pack up while we started pre-departure checks. Then the boat began telling the truth. Only one generator would start. The pilothouse engine controls did not work. That left us with only the flybridge and wing station controls available. Then, just to improve the mood, the insurance company informed us that because of the survey report the boat was effectively under harbor arrest until several issues were corrected.

So the simple move to Fort Lauderdale was starting to look a lot more educational than advertised.

To his credit, the engineer went to work and started grinding through problems. Between his repairs and our diagnosis, we reached the point where we believed the boat could safely make the run south under its own power. So with a flare start, we left.

For a while, it actually went smoothly.

Then as we entered Port Everglades, the insurance representative called and told me that because the pilothouse controls were inoperative, we would need to be towed up the New River. Given where we were and the time of day, I told them we would be much better off stopping at a marina on the ICW and arranging a tug in the morning. That seemed like the obviously sane answer.

Instead, I was told we were only cleared to the yard upriver and should go ahead and drive up the river in the dark with questionable controls and only one generator running.

Which was an impressive recommendation.

Fortunately, a few hundred yards past the river entrance, several alarms started going off while we were right in front of Bahia Mar. We treated that as the gift that it was and tied up on the face dock to sort out what turned out to be a very benign alarm. Once we were secure, another call to the insurance company produced a much more rational answer. Suddenly they were perfectly happy for us to stay put and get tugged upriver in the morning.

Then, because some stories insist on making their point twice, the stereo guys showed up bright and early the next day to keep working. The boat might not run properly, but at least it was going to sound fantastic.

That first trip told me a lot about what kind of chapter that boat was going to be. Before we had even made it to the yard, the priorities were already clear. Mechanical soundness could wait. Appearances, or at least the party version of appearances, apparently could not.
